newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French financial markets recover their nerve.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French financial markets recover their nerve.

text.p: After Monday's selling wave, French financial markets recovered their nerve on Tuesday, betting that even if the left won next Sunday's runoff legislative election, there would be no radical change in economic policy.

Shares were up more than half a percentage point after the CAC-40 blue chip index plunged 3.9 percent on Monday -- its biggest one-day dive in four years -- following the left's upset victory in the first round.
The franc also firmed and bond prices were steady.

Analysts said they did not believe Prime Minister Alain Juppe's surprise decision to resign would boost the centre-right's chances in next Sunday's final vote, saying it smacked too much of panic in the ruling coalition's ranks.
But, said one share analyst, "People just figure even if it is the left in power, they will have to follow the discipline imposed by world financial markets."

"There's what they (the Socialists) say and there is the reality. And the reality is that they do not have much money in the public coffers," said another analyst. "The margin for manoeuvre is very slim for the left as for the right."
The blue-chip CAC-40 index tumbled 0.71 percent at the open, but retraced its losses to trade 0.57 percent or 15.13 points higher at 2,669.87 by late afternoon.
Fears that the bourse could be in for another rough day after traders in New York and London returned to their desks following a long weekend failed to materialise.
Traders said French shares were up in line with other European bourses and domestic buyers were back in the market with bargain hunting at lower levels.

Shares in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, rallied 2.22 percent to 175.10 francs after falling on Monday amid fears its privatisation could be scrapped by a Socialist administration. Other privatisation stocks also recovered, such as bank Credit Lyonnais, which jumped 5.83 percent to 225.10 francs.

"There were fears the privatisation programme would have to be stopped but there is a growing realisation a Socialist-led government will also have to sell shares," a trader said. "They will need it for their budget.
The French franc rallied from Monday's low of 3.3784 against the German currency to trade at 3.3757 per mark.

One foreign exchange trader in Paris called the currency market "astonishingly calm. Of course, it could be that the market is not entirely free but we still haven't seen the hand of the Bank of France" buying up francs to support the currency.
Bond and interest futures rose on Juppe's plans announced late on Monday to resign after the second round vote on June 1 but selling by non-residents knocked them from their highs.
"The main point today for people coming back from holiday is they're seeing the headlines in the press the left could win," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.
The June bond future contract was trading up 0.16 point at 128.46, after plunging 0.68 points on Monday.
Analysts said the bond market would likely continue to be supported by domestic investors who took advantage of the rise in yields after the first round to buy bonds along the curve.

Merrill Lynch market strategist Joanne Perez said investors believed "one way or another way we are going to get" to European monetary union but cautioned that the real issue was under what conditions.
President Jacques Chirac, who called the vote in a bid to win a free hand in the run-up to monetary union was due to address the country in a televised speech at 1800 GMT.
But analysts were sceptical that Chirac could rescue the centre-right's chances.

Juppe's decision to resign was "a step in the right direction but far too late, it emphasises the disarray. Why is Juppe unpopular? Not because he's a horrible man but because of the measures the government has introduced," said BZW bond analyst Phyllis Reed.
